from.title: The Cambridge History of Western Music Theory

topics.title: Performance, meter and rhetoric in the history of theory

attachTo.note: Background to the Foundations and Rhythm groups.

points: Improvised counterpoint and divisions were already described in the 16th century (Lusitano 1553, Vicentino 1555, Zarlino 1558; Ortiz 1553).
Mersenne (1636–37) recorded what Parisian performers actually did.
The 18th-century treatises of Couperin, Quantz, C. P. E. Bach and L. Mozart made performance itself a subject of theory.

rules.text: In common time the first and third beats are good (accented), the second and fourth bad; dissonance belongs on good parts only when prepared.

guidelines.text: Phrases are measured in bars like lines of verse; four-bar units are the norm, which may be extended or compressed.
Motives are upbeat-oriented: the weak beat leads into the strong one.
Arrange a piece like an oration: exordium, narratio, propositio, confirmatio, confutatio, peroratio.
Musical figures depart from simple composition for expressive purposes, as rhetorical figures depart from plain speech.

terms.def: Mattheson's musical analogue of a poetic foot.
Koch's phrase units, from smallest to largest.
Riemann's principle that motives begin with an upbeat.
Composition as the making of a finished work (Listenius 1537).
Finding ideas / arranging them / decorating them (with figures).
Doctrine of the affections that music arouses.
